title: Lead me on
hook: the Handbook ends with old lines: Cleanthes asking to be led willingly, Socrates saying they can kill but not harm him (Enchiridion 52–53)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the moving date, and the games that can't be put off. Your line was the contest is now. What did you start? Day three hundred eighty-six.

Most books end with a summary. The handbook ends with a pocketful of old lines. Not Epictetus' own words, but sayings from a poet, a hymn writer and Socrates, the way some people keep a folded note in a wallet. Before he hands them over, there's one last short lesson about why we know so much and do so little. Then the four sayings, to be kept at hand, he says, always. The handbook was made to be carried. These are what he wanted carried last. Today: lead me on.
screen: `THE HANDBOOK ENDS WITH OLD LINES.` → `A FOLDED NOTE IN A WALLET.` → `LEAD ME ON.`

segments.voice: First, three levels. Section fifty-two says philosophy has three parts. The first and most necessary is using the principles: for example, don't lie. The second is the proof: why one shouldn't lie. The third is checking the proofs: what makes a proof, what's true, what's false. The third exists for the second, and the second for the first. But we do the reverse, he says. We spend our time on the third, and so we lie, while being perfectly ready to prove that lying is wrong. Second, the hymn. Then the last section, and the first saying is by Cleanthes, the school's second head. Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you've set me. I'll follow without hesitating. And if I'm unwilling, and turn bad, I'll follow all the same. Seneca put these lines into Latin, and his version ends: the fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling. Third, the poet and the friend. From Euripides: whoever yields well to necessity is wise among us, and knows the things of the gods. And from Socrates, in prison, to his friend Crito: if this pleases the gods, so be it. Fourth, the last line of the book. Socrates again, at his trial: Anytus and Meletus, his accusers, can kill me, but they cannot harm me. That's where the handbook stops. Not with an argument. With a man who knew which part of him was out of anyone's reach. Whether or not you share their picture of Zeus and destiny, the question in these lines stays: when the road goes where you didn't choose, will you walk it, or be dragged?
screen: `USE FIRST, THEN PROOF, THEN LOGIC.` · `CLEANTHES: LEAD ME, ZEUS.` · `EURIPIDES AND CRITO: SO BE IT.` · `THEY CAN KILL ME, NOT HARM ME.` · then, large: `WILLINGLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Of the four sayings, let one stay with you. Lead me on. Yield well to what must be. If it pleases the gods, so be it. They can kill me, but not harm me. Or, if none of these is yours, another old line that has steadied you, from scripture, a poem, or a person you loved. Say it quietly, once. Then say it again, slower. Let it settle like a stone in a pocket. The bell holds the time.
Cleanthes. Author of the hymn that opens the handbook's last section: lead me, and I'll follow willingly. The fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling. Today's word.
Your line: willingly. Say one line that steadies you today, when the road turns somewhere you didn't choose, and walk it willingly. Day three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism memorize a few short lines, such as the closing sayings of the Enchiridion, and repeat them in hard moments.

original.note: Latin, Seneca's Letter 107: the fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling.

trapdoor: what you thought: go with the flow.
what it means: when the road turns, choose to walk it rather than be dragged, and know what no one can touch.
what a scholar hears: Cleanthes' hymn, Euripides, Plato's Crito and Apology, the four sayings that close the handbook, after the three parts of philosophy.

notes: Enchiridion 52 paraphrased: three topics (use of precepts, demonstrations, confirmation and analysis); we do the reverse and lie while ready to prove we shouldn't. Enchiridion 53: Cleanthes' 'Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny...'; Euripides fragment on yielding to necessity; Crito 43d 'if so it pleases the gods, so let it be'; Apology 30c–d 'Anytus and Meletus can kill me but cannot harm me'. All paraphrased. Long's chapter numbering may differ (he may combine 52–53); confirm.
Seneca, Letter 107.11: Latin translation of Cleanthes ending 'ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt'. Confirm the Latin and that the line is Seneca's addition.
Cleanthes as second head of the Stoic school: confirm.
